decisions.reason: Because the study is a digital re-analysis of the same 11 Racine plays examined by Spitzer (1931 [1928]) before expanding to a comparative corpus, its study type is reproduction, requiring the two-part reproduction outcome schema rather than a single replication outcome string. Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, so exact computational reproduction of original numerical outputs was not checked. In the first phase re-analyzing the original 11 Racine plays via formal CQP queries in TXM on annotated texts, 24 of the roughly 50 stylistic patterns identified by Spitzer could be formally modeled (making the methodological transposition of the full 50-pattern catalog only partially feasible), and for those modeled patterns the analysis verified Spitzer's cited examples and showed that the dampening patterns are even more frequent in Racine's work than Spitzer showed (robust). The subsequent finding that these patterns occur at similar rates in contemporaries—making classical dampening a genre/period style rather than a unique authorial signature—relies on a newly introduced comparative corpus of 38 contemporary plays and does not negate the confirmation of the patterns' prevalence within Racine's plays.

prior_decisions.quote: Regarding Racine and the Classical Age, it has become apparent that the stylistic patterns identified by Leo Spitzer, and which in the aggregate produce a dampening effect, again according to Spitzer, are even more frequent in Racine’s work than Spitzer showed. In addition, the analysis was able to show that these patterns are present in varying degrees in Racine’s work and in the work of his contemporaries, but without very strong (or statistically significant) differences, for the most part. The dampening effect, if understood as the aggregate use of individual stylistic patterns, is therefore clearly not an authorial signature style, but the mark of an entire literary genre during a certain period, at the very least.
prior_decisions.reason: Because Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, reproducing original numerical outputs was outside the analysis plan (not checked), while the computational re-analysis and comparative evaluation substantively qualify Spitzer's interpretation of the dampening effect as a distinctive Racinian signature style (robustness challenges).
